items.question: Does the viewer commit to a wrong answer before hearing the right one?
items.note: The hook has the viewer call the test ('your few-week price test said the new price worked') and the 'let them be wrong' beat states the before-and-after comparison fairly, in his words, as the sane thing every tool suggests, before the crack lands.

items.question: Is there a concrete number in the first sentence?
Is the title's promise fully delivered?
items.note: 'Told you nothing' is delivered as the few-week test sitting below the fit's own bar of {{el_min_periods}} months and {{el_min_price_cv}} of movement: not a wide answer, no answer. 'The sample size you needed' is delivered as the ladder {{n_for_se_half}}, {{n_for_se_quarter}}, {{n_for_se_tenth}} months. Note for the founder: the sample size is in months of price history for one product's fit, not orders in a split test; the script says so plainly, and it is the number the engine computes.

items.question: Does any notation appear before its intuition?
items.note: No symbols anywhere. Elasticity is named as the fitted line is drawn and glossed at once as units falling faster than price rises; standard error is named after the tilting-line picture; false discovery rate is named after the sweep's flags and the null runs; the log-log slope is given only in the close as the how-to.

items.question: Is there exactly one idea, and exactly one CTA?
items.note: One idea: a short price test cannot know whether the price change worked, because the answer is a range and the range is wide. Chapter 2's false-discovery turn is the same idea across a catalog. One CTA, subscribe.

items.question: Does the CTA match the awareness stage in §8?
Is there one claim a competent operator could dispute?
items.note: 'Nearly every price test an operator has ever called a win was noise' and 'products don't live that long' are both disputable and specific.

items.question: Is there any gap over 40 seconds without a re-hook?
Does every number name its model run?
items.note: every chart beat names its run; every key exists

items.question: Is any step of the method withheld?
items.note: The whole method is given: write down the range, move the price on purpose inside {{pm_step_cap}} over enough months, decide on the range not the point, keep a control product as the noise floor, and fit the log-log slope with its standard error in a spreadsheet. The robust errors and the null calibration are described as what the model does rather than as a procedure, which is the honest limit's job under §7, not a withheld step.

items.question: Does the close state a real limitation rather than pitch?
items.note: The close says what the viewer can do (one product's fit, an afternoon on the top products), where it breaks (every product, every month, robust errors, {{null_replicates}} null runs), and that the gap is a model. No service is named and nothing is pitched.

items.question: Are CLIP markers placed, with at least three usable?
Would a $30M founder outside Amazon still get something from this? (pillars 1–2 exempt)
items.note: Universal for anyone who runs a price or A/B test: the width of the answer, how slowly it narrows, and false winners across many tests. The example catalog is Amazon-shaped but nothing in the argument is. Weakness to note: the 'let them be wrong' beat wants a real price-test dashboard screenshot, which the founder has to supply.
